note: What this file is: chapter 1's narration rewritten for a steady New Zealand accent and no shouting (log 09). Same words as chapter-1-narration.json, but: every page opens with the same accent instruction and has no other delivery cues (the old cues - [urgent], [wry], [serious] and so on - moved the voice up and down between pages); no words in capitals (capitals make the voice push); [pause] cues replaced by ellipses; Mattei written in English sounds (muh-TAY-ee) instead of Italian ones.
accent_instruction: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent]

pages.name: the speech
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] You've heard the speech. Times are tough. Tighten your belts. Cut spending, push up interest rates, hold wages down. Sounds like common sense... But austerity has a birthday. Economist Clara E. /məˈteɪi/ dug through the archives and found it, right after the First World War. And she argues it was never really about budgets. It was about stopping something.

pages.name: the war
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Picture Britain in 1915. The war is burning through shells faster than factories can make them. And the government doesn't run out of money... It runs out of shells. So it takes charge: what factories make, what things cost, what workers are paid. Italy does the same. And people notice. If the economy can be organised for war... why not for what people need, instead of just for profit?

pages.name: Britain after the war
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] When the war ends, workers don't want to go back. In Britain, union membership doubles, to eight million. In Glasgow, sixty thousand people pack a square, demanding a shorter working week. The government sends in troops... And tanks. Coal miners demand public ownership of the mines. A royal commission backs them. The government ignores it.

pages.name: Italy
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] In Italy, it goes further. In 1919, more than a million workers go on strike. In 1920, half a million take over their factories.

pages.name: the capital order
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] Now look at it from the owners' side. This isn't just about pay. It threatens what /məˈteɪi/ calls the capital order: a few people own the land, the factories and the mines... and everyone else must work for a wage to survive. If workers can run things themselves, that order could fall.

pages.name: the experts
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So the experts get together. Brussels, 1920: thirty-nine countries send delegates, mostly bankers and treasury officials. Guess who isn't in the room? Not one trade unionist. Genoa, 1922: same advice. And it's simple. Balance the budget. Cut public spending. Stop creating new money. Hand interest rates to central banks, out of reach of voters. And get back on gold.

pages.name: three parts
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] /məˈteɪi/ says the plan has three parts. Spending: cut public services, and tax everyday purchases instead of wealth. Money: make borrowing expensive, so businesses slow down and jobs disappear. Work: cut wages, sell off what the public owns, weaken the unions.

pages.name: the official story
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] The official story sounds reasonable. Prices are rising, war debts are huge, and a government, like a household, has to balance its books. Right? But economists who study how modern money works say a country that issues its own money isn't a household. It can't run out of its own money. It can run out of workers, materials and machines, as the war just showed. And gold? Gold was a limit they chose. Going back to it meant forcing wages and prices down.

pages.name: why
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So why do it? Ask /məˈteɪi/, and her answer is blunt: power. Take away the alternatives, like public housing and help for the unemployed, and people must take whatever job is going, at whatever wage. The message to workers: work more, consume less.

pages.name: sound familiar
pages.text: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] That's the argument /məˈteɪi/ makes. Austerity was never really about the books. It was about power... Sound familiar? But wait. If a country can't run out of its own money... won't creating it just cause inflation? That's next.
